topic: The Transformational View of Derivatives: From Slope to Scaling
target_audience: University students and advanced high school students with basic calculus knowledge

outline.topic: The Transformational View of Derivatives: From Slope to Scaling
outline.target_audience: University students and advanced high school students with basic calculus knowledge

sections.title: The Hook: Meet Rex the Rubber Dinosaur
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a derivative not as a static slope on a graph, but as a dynamic 'stretch factor'. Use an animation of a character that changes shape to visualize transformation.
sections.example: Imagine 'Rex', a rubber dinosaur standing on a number line. As he moves from point A to point B, his body stretches or compresses according to a mathematical function. If Rex moves 1 unit but his tail stretches 3 units, something powerful is happening at that specific location.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Mapping View
sections.content: Transition from the standard XY-plane (Cartesian) to a 'Mapping View'. Draw two parallel number lines: the Input space (x) and the Output space (f(x)). Show how points on the top line map to points on the bottom line via 'light rays'.
sections.example: For the function f(x) = 3x, visualize arrows connecting x=1 to f(x)=3, and x=2 to f(x)=6. Observe that the space between the arrows on the output line is exactly 3 times wider than the input line.

sections.title: The Local Zoom: Linear Approximation
sections.content: Focus on a non-linear function. Explain that globally, the 'stretching' varies, but if we zoom in infinitely on a specific point, the transformation looks like a constant scaling. This is the essence of local linearity.
sections.example: Take f(x) = x². At x=2, zoom in on a tiny segment 'dx'. Watch as the output segment 'df' becomes a straight line mapping. Through the lens, the transformation looks like a simple magnifying glass.

sections.title: Defining the Derivative as a Scaling Factor
sections.content: Define f'(x) as the ratio of the output segment length to the input segment length (df/dx). Emphasize that if f'(x) > 1, the space is stretching; if 0 < f'(x) < 1, it is shrinking; if f'(x) < 0, the space is being flipped (mirrored).
sections.example: At x=3 for f(x)=x², f'(3)=6. This means a tiny interval of 0.01 around x=3 is stretched 6 times larger to become 0.06 in the output space. Visualize this as a 'local speed limit' for how fast the output moves relative to the input.

sections.title: Application: The Magnifying Glass Effect
sections.content: Consolidate the knowledge by applying the transformational view to a real-world device simulation. Show how derivatives help in computer graphics to distort textures without losing local proportions.
sections.example: Imagine a digital magnifying glass moving over a map. The derivative at the center of the glass tells the computer exactly how much to 'scale' the pixels of the map to create a smooth, zoomed-in image. If the derivative is 2, every pixel is doubled in width locally.

storyboard.title: The Hook: Meet Rex the Rubber Dinosaur
lecture_lines: Meet Rex, a rubber dinosaur on a number line.
As Rex moves, his body stretches or compresses.
One step forward might stretch his tail three units.
This isn't just a slope on a static graph.
It's a local stretch factor at a specific point.
animations: A simple vector dinosaur 'Rex' appears on a white horizontal number line.
Rex moves along the line, and his torso elongates or squishes dynamically to show transformation.
Highlight Rex's tail extending significantly as he takes a step, using a #00FF00 glow.
A static XY graph appears briefly and fades out, shifting focus back to Rex's motion.
A label 'Stretch Factor' appears above Rex at a specific position, highlighted in #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Mapping View
lecture_lines: Imagine two parallel lines for input and output.
Connect inputs to outputs using mapping arrows.
For f(x) equals 3x, arrows spread out wider.
The output space stretches relative to the input.
This mapping view shows how functions transform space.
animations: Two parallel horizontal lines (Input x, Output f(x)) appear in #FFFFFF.
Multiple thin grey arrows connect evenly spaced points on the top line to the bottom line.
For f(x)=3x, arrows from x=1 and x=2 connect to f(x)=3 and f(x)=6 in #00FFFF.
Highlight the segment between 3 and 6 on the output line in #00FF00, showing it is 3x wider.
Animate a set of input points 'blooming' into a larger output range to show space transformation.

storyboard.title: The Local Zoom: Linear Approximation
lecture_lines: Non-linear functions stretch space differently at each point.
Let's zoom into a single point on a curve.
Locally, every smooth transformation looks like constant scaling.
A tiny input interval maps to an output interval.
Zooming in makes any curve look perfectly linear.
animations: Display the mapping of f(x)=x^2 between two number lines with non-linear arrow spacing.
Highlight a tiny interval 'dx' around x=2 on the Input line in #FFD700.
Show the corresponding interval 'df' on the Output line, which is roughly 4 times larger.
Animate a 'Zoom' effect into the intervals, making the mapping arrows look parallel and straight.
Label the zoomed view 'Local Linearity' and highlight the region boundary in #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Defining the Derivative as a Scaling Factor
lecture_lines: The derivative measures the local scaling ratio.
Values above one stretch space; below one shrink it.
Negative derivatives flip the direction of the output.
animations: The formula f'(x) = df/dx appears in the center of the screen in #FFFFFF.
A scaling gauge shifts between a 'Stretch' zone (>1) and a 'Shrink' zone (<1) in #00FF00.
Arrows cross between the input and output lines, labeled 'Flipped' in #FF00FF for negative values.

storyboard.title: Application: The Magnifying Glass Effect
lecture_lines: This view helps computers distort textures for graphics.
Digital magnifying glasses scale pixels using local derivatives.
Derivatives ensure smooth and accurate visual scaling.
animations: A grid representing a digital texture appears, with a magnifying glass moving across it.
A single grid cell under the glass is highlighted in #00FFFF and expands by a factor of 2.
The text 'f'(x) = 2.0' follows the magnifying glass, representing the local scale factor.
